If dividend growth becomes a weaker or noisier proxy for durable cash generation, the strategy's purported edge vanishes and selections perform no better than neutral benchmarks.
flaws.question: How robust is the strategy to changes in corporate payout behavior (e.g., lower dividend issuance, substitution by buybacks, more frequent special dividends) and what contingency rules would you apply?

flaws.title: High: Investors want present yield and stability, not historical growth rates
flaws.description: Failure scenario: potential outside investors read the white paper and want dividend strategies for cash income or low volatility; they discover the portfolio’s current yield or income volatility is lower/higher than expected because the screen optimizes five‑year growth, not yield. Stated interest in 'dividend strategies' therefore fails to convert into committed capital and the attempt to scale via published research stalls.
flaws.question: Have you validated that your target allocators prioritize five‑year dividend growth over current yield, dividend stability, or downside protection, and are willing to accept the strategy's income profile?

flaws.title: Medium: Backtest period and S&P‑only universe may reflect favorable past regimes
flaws.description: Failure scenario: the 2005–2024 window and restriction to S&P 500 survivals coincided with regimes (recoveries, falling rates, sector composition) that favored dividend growers; a different future regime (higher rates, sector rotation, persistent low growth) reverses the relationship and the strategy underperforms. If the strategy's edge was regime‑dependent, next 18 months of different macro conditions erode returns.
flaws.question: How does the strategy perform in rolling, out‑of‑sample slices and in simulated adverse macro regimes (rising rates, stagflation, sector rotations)?

flaws.title: Medium: Dividend data quirks—specials, one‑offs, restatements and corporate actions—could fake growth
flaws.description: Failure scenario: special dividends, one‑time payouts, spin‑offs, or restated histories inflate five‑year growth rates in backtest data but are hard to identify in real time, causing the live rule to pick names whose apparent growth was not repeatable. If these anomalies are common among top-ranked names, the subsequent dividend path disappoints and performance degrades.
flaws.question: What real‑time filters and data‑cleaning rules will you implement to exclude special/one‑time payouts, spin‑offs, and restatements from the five‑year growth signal?

evidence_audit.summary: Evidence base: Mixed. The backtest shows historical outperformance on the authors' constructed universe, but key measurement and sourcing issues remain. The most important unresolved problems are the arithmetic contradiction in reported CAGR vs terminal wealth and survivorship/look-ahead and implementation assumptions that could materially change results.

flaws.title: Arithmetic contradiction between stated CAGR and terminal wealth
flaws.description: You report a 14.2% annual return for the screen and also say $100,000 in Jan 2005 would grow to just under $1.9M by end-2024. These cannot both be true: 100,000*(1.142)^20 ≈ $1.42M, while 100,000*(1.1586)^20 ≈ $1.9M, so $1.9M corresponds to ≈15.86% p.a., not 14.2%. The benchmark figure is internally consistent (100,000*(1.098)^20 ≈ $650k), which isolates the contradiction to the screen numbers.
flaws.question: Provide the exact annualized return you computed for the screen, the per-year return series or yearly ending values, and reconcile which of the two reported facts (14.2% p.a. or final wealth ≈ $1.9M) is correct and how the other arose (rounding, typo, or different compounding convention).

flaws.title: Universe construction causes survivorship bias (using 'today's S&P 500' tickers)
flaws.description: You backtested on the 480 stocks in today's S&P 500 with complete price histories over 2005–2024, which excludes firms that were in the index earlier but delisted or replaced. That selection mechanically removes losers and firms with interrupted dividend histories and thus inflates historical returns. This is a load-bearing choice because it directly affects realized returns and drawdowns.
flaws.question: Provide the exact ticker list used and rerun the backtest on the historical S&P 500 constituents (or a full investable universe including delistings/mergers) for 2005–2024 and report the same metrics so we can compare survivorship-free results.

flaws.title: Possible look-ahead or timing error in dividend-growth and payout-ratio inputs
flaws.description: The rule uses 'five-year dividend growth' and current payout ratio < 60%. The backtest must ensure both metrics are computed only from information that would have been available at each January rebalance (e.g., trailing 5 years of declared dividends and the latest reported payout ratio as of that date). If you used revised/annualized trailing figures or end-of-sample restated financials, the result could leak future information into past dates and overstate performance.
flaws.question: For each rebalance date provide the exact formulas and raw input fields (dividend per share by declaration date or record date, EPS used for payout ratio, source and timestamp), and confirm that only data available as of that rebalance date were used; if not, produce a version that enforces strict vintage/timestamped inputs.

flaws.title: Unspecified turnover and trading-cost methodology behind the '10 bps' assumption
flaws.description: You state assumed trading costs of 10 basis points per rebalance but give no turnover, slippage, or how costs were applied (per side, per share, on full turnover). Trading-costs interact with turnover — e.g., assuming (not from document) 100% turnover at each annual rebalance: 0.001 × 20 rebalances = 2.0% cumulative cost; with partial turnover it differs. Without turnover and implementation rules the post-cost returns are not verifiable.
flaws.question: Provide the average turnover (percent of portfolio traded) per rebalance over the backtest, and the exact formula you used to convert that and the 10 bps into a drag on annual return (including whether 10 bps is per side or round-trip and whether it was applied to pre- or post-dividend values).

flaws.title: Sensitivity claims (50/60/70% cutoffs) lack supporting statistics
flaws.description: You assert results were 'similar' for payout-ratio cutoffs of 50, 60 and 70 percent but provide no outcome table. Sensitivity of returns, volatility, drawdown and annual win-count to that parameter is load-bearing for claims of robustness.
flaws.question: Supply a table showing annualized return, volatility, max drawdown, and number of years beating the benchmark for payout cutoffs 50%, 60%, and 70% so we can judge the stated robustness.

flaws.title: No disclosure of dividend reinvestment, corporate actions, or treatment of delistings
flaws.description: The screen is dividend-focused but you do not state whether dividends were reinvested, how special dividends were handled, or how delisted companies were treated (cash-out at last price, zero recovery, etc.). Those choices materially change terminal wealth and drawdowns.
flaws.question: Confirm whether dividends were reinvested and provide the rules used for special dividends, stock splits, spin-offs and for companies that were delisted (including recovery assumptions); if not already done, produce a version with standard investable assumptions (dividends reinvested at next-trade price and delistings treated conservatively).

pre_mortem.summary: The likeliest failure is a false positive driven by stopping the experiment early during an atypical three-day-sale/email window; the p≈0.02 from a standard two-proportion test is not reliable under daily peeking and an unusual traffic mix. Secondary failures include unmeasured heterogeneity by traffic source (email vs. organic/paid), small sample winner's-curse effects that shrink with scale, unjustified linear scaling to monthly/other pages, and process/incentive choices that remove replication safeguards.

flaws.title: Critical: Early stopping during a sale/email window produced a transient false positive
flaws.description: Failure scenario: the team checked results daily and stopped on day 9 while a three-day weekend sale email had been sent on day 6, so the observed lift could be a transient response to the sale rather than a durable design effect. The likeliest way this fails is that the sale-driven, high-intent visitors boosted conversion for a brief window and the apparent lift disappears or reverses when the redesign is exposed to normal traffic. Because the team explicitly decided not to run a follow-up, there is no guardrail to detect regression to baseline before widespread rollout and bonus allocation.
flaws.question: How would the effect estimate change in a pre-registered, fully powered test that excludes the sale/email cohort or controls for it, run without interim peeking?

flaws.title: High: Unsegmented traffic creates confounding by email/high-intent visitors
flaws.description: Failure scenario: email recipients (or other high-intent channels) responded much better to the new checkout, and even a small imbalance or interaction produced the bulk of the lift despite the dashboard summary. The likeliest way this fails is that the design only helps a specific source (email during promotions) and provides little or no uplift for the majority of organic, paid, or returning visitors once rolled out. Because no per-source breakdown was pre-specified, the team may have misattributed a channel effect to a UI change.
flaws.question: Can you show variant-level conversion broken down by traffic source with sufficient sample and confirm randomization held within each source?

flaws.title: High: Sequential peeking invalidated the standard p-value
flaws.description: Failure scenario: daily checks and stopping at an apparently low p-value introduced optional stopping bias, so the reported p≈0.02 from a standard two-proportion test understates the true Type I error. The likeliest way this fails is that the statistical significance vanishes once the analysis accounts for multiple looks or uses a sequential testing framework, revealing the result was a false positive. The team's statement that 'it was already significant' relies on an analysis method that the experiment process did not support.
flaws.question: Have you recomputed significance using an appropriate sequential testing correction or confidence sequence, and does the effect survive that correction?

flaws.title: Medium: Small sample and winner’s curse inflate the observed lift
flaws.description: Failure scenario: with only ~2,100 visitors per arm the observed 37% relative lift is an upward-biased estimate (winner's curse), and as the variant sees tens of thousands of users the measured effect regresses toward a much smaller true lift or zero. The likeliest way this fails is that projected monthly/annual revenue gains are based on an overestimate that collapses under larger, more stable samples. Without post-hoc uncertainty quantification of the true effect size range, the revenue extrapolation is fragile.
flaws.question: What are the post-hoc confidence intervals for the true effect size and what sample would be required to obtain a stable estimate at the targeted MDE?

flaws.title: Medium: Assumption that checkout lift scales linearly and transfers to product pages
flaws.description: Failure scenario: the team extrapolated a short-term checkout lift to monthly revenue and green-lit the same redesign for the product page without evidence that the mechanisms (purchase intent, urgency, funnel position) are the same. The likeliest way this fails is that product pages and steady-state traffic have different drivers, so applying the same change yields little benefit or negative interactions, while the monthly extrapolation magnifies any initial overestimate into a large mistaken forecast.
flaws.question: What empirical or theoretical justification do you have that the checkout effect will scale linearly to the full monthly funnel and that the same design will produce comparable gains on product pages?

flaws.title: Low: Incentives and decision rules removed replication and encouraged premature declaration
flaws.description: Failure scenario: declaring the test a win, shipping immediately, and crediting the project in the bonus pool created incentives to stop early and avoid replication, making retraction politically costly if the effect vanishes. The likeliest way this fails is organizational — reversal or additional testing is delayed or resisted, so a transient result becomes entrenched as policy and budget allocation despite not replicating at scale.
flaws.question: Who approved the stopping rule and bonus recognition, and will you require an independent, pre-registered replication before embedding the result in bonuses and cross-funnel rollouts?

evidence_audit.summary: Evidence base: Mixed. The team ran a live A/B test on their operating site and measured a conversion uplift, so real traction exists. However the experiment was stopped early during a sale period without pre-specified stopping rules, source-level breakdowns, or power/MDE planning, leaving the p-value and the annual revenue extrapolation unreliable.

flaws.title: Stopping the test early after daily peeking invalidates the reported p-value
flaws.description: You report checking results daily and stopping on day 9 once the new design “pulled clearly ahead.” Multiple interim looks inflate the Type I error: a nominal two-proportion test p≈0.02 is not valid unless a sequential testing correction or pre-specified stopping rule was used. With n_old=2,150 and n_new=2,130 and the observed z≈2.30 (two-sided p≈0.02), an uncorrected p at a single look is misleading if you looked daily up to day 9.
flaws.question: Provide either the pre-specified stopping rule/alpha-spending plan used before the test started, or recompute the test result with an appropriate sequential correction (e.g. O'Brien–Fleming / alpha-spending or an exact adjustment for the number and timing of interim looks) — after that correction, does the effect remain statistically significant?

flaws.title: A three-day sale email during the window is a plausible confound and was not quantified
flaws.description: Day 9 includes a three-day weekend sale email sent on day 6; you did not segment by traffic source. Even if the dashboard says both versions received a 'similar share' of email traffic, without per-arm counts the sale could differentially inflate conversions. The test sample (2,130/2,150 visitors) is small and concentrated around the sale period, so traffic mix bias is material.
flaws.question: Provide per-arm counts and conversions for visitors attributed to the sale email (and for other traffic sources) and the day-by-day visitor/conversion table for each arm so we can recompute the lift excluding email-driven traffic and check for day-level spikes.

flaws.title: Extrapolating the 9‑day result to monthly/annual revenue ignores sampling uncertainty
flaws.description: You extrapolate the observed lift to 60,000 monthly visitors to claim +$57,600/month and ~$691k/year. The test used 4,280 visitors (≈7.1% of monthly traffic) and the observed absolute lift is ≈1.493 percentage points. The 95% CI for the absolute lift from the test data is about 0.22% to 2.77% (0.01493 ± 1.96×0.006497 = [0.0022,0.02766]). That maps to monthly extra orders ≈132 to 1,659 and monthly revenue uplift ≈$8.4k to $106k, a very wide range that includes outcomes much smaller than your headline.
flaws.question: Provide the 95% confidence interval for the absolute and relative lift and show the revenue-upside range when applying those bounds to 60,000 visitors (or provide the post-launch 30-day conversion data to validate the point estimate empirically).

flaws.title: No power/MDE or planned-sample calculation was presented for the 28‑day test
flaws.description: You planned a 28-day test but do not state the planned sample size, minimum detectable effect (MDE), or target alpha/power. Without that, it's impossible to judge whether the stopped test was underpowered or whether the observed effect was larger than expected. This matters to interpreting both significance and business impact.
flaws.question: Provide the pre-test power calculation (planned sample size, MDE at the chosen alpha and power) for the 28-day test, or if none was done, compute the MDE you would have powered to with full 28 days of typical traffic.
